specStatements.text: A lens forms an image by refracting light. In a convex lens, parallel rays of light are brought to a focus at the principal focus. The distance from the lens to the principal focus is called the focal length. Ray diagrams are used to show the formation of images by convex and concave lenses.
The image produced by a convex lens can be either real or virtual. The image produced by a concave lens is always virtual.
Students should be able to construct ray diagrams to illustrate the similarities and differences between convex and concave lenses.
The magnification produced by a lens can be calculated using the equation:
Magnification is a ratio and so has no units.
Image height and object height should both be measured in either mm or cm.

A concave lens will be represented by:

scopeNotes.statement: Magnification is a ratio and so has no units.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every magnification in this material is written as a bare number — 3, 0.3, 2 — and never carries cm, mm or any other unit. Where a question offers a magnification with a unit attached it is always a distractor, and the rationale states explicitly that dividing a height by a height cancels the unit. No item asks the student to give a unit for magnification, and no correct answer supplies one.

scopeNotes.statement: Image height and object height should both be measured in either mm or cm.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: All heights used are given in mm or in cm and in no other unit. Where a question deliberately supplies one height in mm and the other in cm, the required step is to convert so that both are in the same one of those two units before dividing; metres, inches and mixed-unit answers never appear as the correct response.

Magnification is calculated only from image height and object height, exactly as the specification writes the equation. No item uses image distance or object distance to find magnification, and the lens formula relating object distance, image distance and focal length is not used anywhere, because the specification gives magnification in terms of heights alone.

concepts.definition: An optical component, usually of glass or plastic, that forms an image by refracting light. The light is refracted as it enters the lens and again as it leaves, and this change of direction is what brings the rays together or spreads them apart.

A lens that is thicker in the middle than at its edges. Parallel rays of light passing through a convex lens are brought to a focus at the principal focus, so a convex lens is also called a converging lens.

The point at which parallel rays of light are brought to a focus by a convex lens. For a concave lens, parallel rays are spread out so that they appear to come from the principal focus on the same side of the lens as the incoming light.

The distance from the lens to the principal focus. A more powerful lens, which bends light more strongly, has a shorter focal length. The focal length is a property of the lens itself and does not change when the object is moved.

The straight line drawn through the centre of the lens at right angles to it. Ray diagrams are set out along the principal axis, with the principal focus marked on it at the focal length from the lens on each side.
A lens that is thinner in the middle than at its edges. It spreads parallel rays of light apart, so it is also called a diverging lens, and the image it produces is always virtual.

A scale drawing that uses at least two rays from a point on the object to show where the image is formed, how big it is and which way up it is. Ray diagrams are used to show the formation of images by convex and concave lenses.

An image formed where rays of light actually meet after passing through the lens. Because the light really is there, a real image can be projected onto a screen. A real image formed by a convex lens is inverted.

An image formed where rays of light only appear to come from, once they are traced back behind the lens. No light actually meets there, so a virtual image cannot be projected onto a screen, although it can be seen by looking through the lens. A virtual image formed by a lens is upright.

concepts.term: Image produced by a convex lens
concepts.definition: It can be either real or virtual. When the object is further from the lens than the principal focus, the refracted rays meet and a real, inverted image is formed. When the object is nearer to the lens than the principal focus, the rays leave still diverging and a virtual, upright, magnified image is formed on the same side as the object.

concepts.term: Image produced by a concave lens
concepts.definition: It is always virtual. The refracted rays always leave the lens diverging, so they never meet; traced back, they appear to come from a point between the lens and the principal focus. The image is upright, smaller than the object and on the same side of the lens as the object.

concepts.term: Constructing a ray diagram for a convex lens
concepts.definition: Draw the lens symbol on the principal axis and mark the principal focus at the focal length on each side. From the top of the object draw a ray parallel to the axis, refracted through the principal focus on the far side, and a ray straight through the centre of the lens, which is undeviated. Where these two rays cross is the top of a real image; if they do not cross, trace them back to find the virtual image.

concepts.term: Constructing a ray diagram for a concave lens
concepts.definition: Draw the lens symbol on the principal axis and mark the principal focus on each side. From the top of the object draw a ray parallel to the axis, which is refracted so that it appears to come from the principal focus on the same side as the object, and a ray straight through the centre of the lens, which is undeviated. Trace the refracted rays back until they meet to locate the virtual image.

Both form images by refracting light, both are drawn on a principal axis with a principal focus at the focal length, and in both the ray through the centre of the lens goes straight on. They differ in what they do to parallel rays: the convex lens brings them to a focus, while the concave lens spreads them apart. Because of this the convex lens can produce a real or a virtual image, whereas the concave lens always produces a virtual one.

The magnification produced by a lens can be calculated using the equation: magnification = (image height)/(object height). This equation is supplied on the AQA Physics equation sheet, so the skill assessed is selecting it and applying it correctly rather than recalling it. A magnification greater than 1 means the image is larger than the object; a magnification less than 1 means it is smaller.

Magnification is a ratio — a height divided by a height — so the units cancel and the answer is a plain number with no unit after it. Writing '3 cm' or '3 mm' for a magnification is wrong; the answer is simply 3.

concepts.term: Measuring image height and object height
concepts.definition: Image height and object height should both be measured in either mm or cm. What matters is that the same unit is used for both, because the ratio is only correct when the two heights are expressed in the same unit; if one is given in mm and the other in cm, convert one of them first.

In ray diagrams a convex lens is represented by a vertical straight line drawn across the principal axis with an arrowhead at each end, both pointing outwards, away from the axis. The outward arrowheads are a reminder that the lens is thicker in the middle.

A concave lens is represented by a vertical straight line drawn across the principal axis with an arrowhead at each end, both pointing inwards, towards the axis. The inward arrowheads are a reminder that the lens is thinner in the middle.

misconceptions.question: Does a lens work like a mirror?
misconceptions.correct: A lens forms an image by refracting light — the light passes through the lens and changes direction.
misconceptions.misconception: A lens bounces light off its shiny surface to make an image, in the same way a mirror does.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Lenses and mirrors are met together in the same topic, both are smooth and shiny, and both produce images that can be described as real or virtual. Students transfer the mechanism they already know from mirrors onto the new object.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is explicit: a lens forms an image by refracting light. Light goes through a lens and is bent as it enters and as it leaves. A little light does reflect off the surfaces, but that is not how the image is formed.

misconceptions.question: Is the principal focus where the image appears?
misconceptions.correct: The principal focus is the point where rays that arrive parallel to the axis are brought to a focus. The image usually forms somewhere else entirely.
misconceptions.misconception: The image always forms at the principal focus, because that is the point where the lens focuses the light.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'focus' is used in everyday speech to mean 'where the picture is sharp', so students read the principal focus as the place a sharp image must appear. The first ray diagrams they see also send one ray through the principal focus, which reinforces the link.
misconceptions.correction: The principal focus is defined only for rays arriving parallel to the axis. Rays from a real object are not parallel, so they meet at a different place. Where the image forms depends on where the object is, but the principal focus stays fixed at the focal length from the lens.

misconceptions.question: Is the focal length the distance from the lens to the image?
misconceptions.correct: The distance from the lens to the principal focus is called the focal length.
misconceptions.misconception: The focal length is how far the image is from the lens, so it changes when I move the object.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In practical work the quantity students actually measure is often a lens-to-screen distance, and when a distant object is used that distance really is close to the focal length. They then generalise it to every object position.
misconceptions.correction: The focal length is a fixed property of the lens: the distance from the lens to the principal focus. Moving the object changes where the image forms but never changes the focal length.

misconceptions.question: Can a concave lens make a real image if the object is far enough away?
misconceptions.correct: The image produced by a concave lens is always virtual.
misconceptions.misconception: If the object is a long way off, a concave lens will bring the light together and make a real image, just as a convex lens does.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that the image from a convex lens changes as the object is moved, and assume the concave lens must behave the same way at some object distance. The word 'lens' carries the expectation of focusing.
misconceptions.correction: A concave lens spreads light apart at every object distance, so the refracted rays never meet and can never form an image on a screen. The specification states without exception that the image produced by a concave lens is always virtual.

misconceptions.question: If I can see the image, does that make it real?
misconceptions.correct: A virtual image can be seen by looking through the lens; what makes an image real is that light rays actually meet where the image is, so it can be caught on a screen.
misconceptions.misconception: A virtual image is one that cannot be seen at all, so any image I can actually look at must be a real image.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday meaning of 'virtual' is 'not actually there', which students take to mean invisible. The magnifying glass they use every day gives a virtual image that is perfectly easy to see, so the label feels wrong.
misconceptions.correction: Real and virtual describe where the light goes, not whether the eye can see it. For a virtual image the rays only appear to come from the image position, so no light arrives at a screen placed there — but the eye, looking through the lens, sees it clearly.

misconceptions.question: Does a convex lens always give a real, inverted image?
misconceptions.correct: The image produced by a convex lens can be either real or virtual, depending on where the object is placed.
misconceptions.misconception: A convex lens always turns the picture upside down and always makes an image you could put on a screen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Almost every ray diagram students draw first has the object outside the principal focus, which does give a real, inverted image. The one case that behaves differently, the magnifying glass, is rarely drawn as a ray diagram.
misconceptions.correction: When the object is nearer to the lens than the principal focus, the refracted rays leave the lens still spreading apart. They never meet, so the image is virtual, upright and magnified. That is exactly how a magnifying glass is used.

misconceptions.question: Is the ray aimed at the centre of the lens refracted like the others?
misconceptions.correct: The ray drawn from the top of the object to the centre of the lens carries straight on without changing direction.
misconceptions.misconception: Every ray that meets a lens has to be bent, so the middle ray must be bent towards the principal focus too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are taught that a lens refracts light, and apply that rule to all rays without exception. The reason the central ray is undeviated — the two surfaces are effectively parallel there, so the small sideways shift is ignored — is not obvious from the drawing.
misconceptions.correction: At the centre of the lens the front and back surfaces are parallel, so the ray emerges travelling in its original direction. In ray diagrams the central ray is always drawn as a straight line through the lens, and it is that straight ray which fixes the size and position of the image.

misconceptions.question: For a concave lens, where does a ray parallel to the axis go?
misconceptions.correct: It is refracted so that it spreads away from the axis, along a line that traced backwards passes through the principal focus on the same side as the object.
misconceptions.misconception: The parallel ray goes through the principal focus on the far side of the lens, the same as it does for a convex lens.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The convex ray rule is learned first and thoroughly, and the concave diagram looks superficially the same — a line, an axis, a focus marked on each side. Students reuse the rule they know.
misconceptions.correction: A concave lens diverges light, so the refracted ray moves away from the axis. To find the image the diverging ray must be traced backwards, and that construction line passes through the principal focus on the object side. This is why the image is virtual.

misconceptions.question: What unit should a magnification be given in?
misconceptions.correct: None. Magnification is a ratio and so has no units.
misconceptions.misconception: Magnification is worked out from heights in centimetres, so the answer must be in centimetres too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are trained, correctly, to put a unit on every answer, and are penalised when they leave one off. Nothing in the calculation looks different from the ones where a unit is needed.
misconceptions.correction: The equation divides a height by a height. If both are in cm, the cm cancel and a pure number is left. The specification says directly that magnification is a ratio and so has no units, so writing a unit after it is wrong.

misconceptions.question: Which way round does the magnification equation go?
misconceptions.misconception: Magnification is the object height divided by the image height, because you start with the object.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students order the two quantities in the order the story happens — object first, then image — rather than in the order the equation states. The two heights are so similar in kind that neither position feels obviously wrong.
misconceptions.correction: The equation is given as magnification = (image height)/(object height): the image height goes on top. Using it upside down turns every enlargement into a number below 1 and every reduction into a number above 1, which is a useful check.

misconceptions.question: Does it matter if one height is in mm and the other in cm?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Image height and object height should both be measured in either mm or cm — the same unit for both.
misconceptions.misconception: The units cancel anyway because magnification has no units, so I can divide a height in cm by a height in mm.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly learn that magnification has no unit, and then reason backwards that the units cannot matter at all. The cancelling only works when the two units are identical, which is easy to miss.
misconceptions.correction: Units cancel only when they are the same. Dividing 8.0 cm by 40 mm as though the numbers alone mattered gives 0.2 instead of the correct 2 — wrong by a factor of ten. Convert first so that both heights are in mm, or both in cm.

misconceptions.question: Which lens has the arrowheads pointing inwards?
misconceptions.correct: The symbol with both arrowheads pointing inwards, towards the axis, is the concave lens; outward arrowheads mean a convex lens.
misconceptions.misconception: Inward arrowheads mean a convex lens, because a convex lens brings the rays inwards to a focus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look for meaning in the symbol and find a tempting one: arrows pointing in must mean light being brought in. The convention actually follows the shape of the lens, not what it does to light.
misconceptions.correction: The arrowheads follow the cross-section of the lens. A convex lens is thicker in the middle, so its arrowheads point outwards; a concave lens is thinner in the middle, so its arrowheads point inwards. Reading the symbol by shape gives the right answer every time.

misconceptions.question: Can the magnification be less than 1?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A magnification less than 1 simply means the image is smaller than the object.
misconceptions.misconception: Magnification means making things bigger, so the answer always has to be greater than 1; a value below 1 means I have made a mistake.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday word 'magnify' means 'enlarge', so a magnification below 1 sounds self-contradictory. Students who get 0.3 assume they have inverted the equation and turn it upside down.
misconceptions.correction: In physics magnification is just the ratio of the two heights. Above 1 the image is enlarged, below 1 it is diminished, and exactly 1 means it is the same size. A concave lens always gives a magnification below 1.

misconceptions.question: Which way up is the image from a concave lens?
misconceptions.correct: It is upright — the same way up as the object — as well as being virtual and smaller.
misconceptions.misconception: The image from a concave lens is upside down, because lenses turn images over.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The inverted image from a convex lens is the first and most memorable result students meet, and it becomes their idea of what a lens does. Ray diagrams for concave lenses are drawn far less often.
misconceptions.correction: Tracing the diverging rays back places the image on the same side of the axis as the object, so it is upright. Only a real image formed by a convex lens is inverted, and a concave lens never forms a real image.

misconceptions.question: Is the focal length how far away you hold the object?
misconceptions.correct: The focal length is the distance from the lens to the principal focus, and it does not depend on the object at all.
misconceptions.misconception: The focal length is how far from the lens you have to put the object to get a sharp picture.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The experience of focusing a camera or a magnifying glass is one of moving things until the picture is sharp, so 'focal' becomes attached to the object distance the student adjusts.
misconceptions.correction: The focal length is fixed by the lens itself, and is defined by rays arriving parallel to the axis being brought to a focus at the principal focus. The object distance that gives a sharp image is a separate quantity that changes from one situation to another.

misconceptions.question: Where in a lens is the light refracted?
misconceptions.correct: At both surfaces — light is refracted as it enters the lens and again as it leaves it.
misconceptions.misconception: The light travels straight through the glass and is only bent at the surface where it comes out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams of lenses usually show only the incoming ray and the final outgoing ray, with the path inside the glass hidden by the shading, so students see a single bend at one place.
misconceptions.correction: Refraction happens wherever light crosses a boundary between two materials. It is refracted on entering the glass and again on leaving it, and the two bends together produce the overall change of direction that forms the image.

misconceptions.question: Are virtual images always smaller than the object?
misconceptions.correct: No. A concave lens gives a virtual image that is smaller, but a convex lens used as a magnifying glass gives a virtual image that is larger.
misconceptions.misconception: Virtual means the image is not properly there, so it is always a small, faint version of the object.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The concave lens result — virtual, upright, diminished — is often the only virtual image drawn in full, so its three properties are remembered as a single package that belongs to all virtual images.
misconceptions.correction: 'Virtual' says only that the rays appear to come from the image and that it cannot be caught on a screen. It says nothing about size. An object placed inside the principal focus of a convex lens gives a virtual image that is bigger than the object.

misconceptions.question: Does a real image have to be the right way up?
misconceptions.correct: No. A real image formed by a convex lens is inverted; being real means the rays actually meet there.
misconceptions.misconception: If the image looks the same way up as the object then it must be the real one, because that is what the object really looks like.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'real' is read as 'true to life'. An upside-down picture looks wrong, so students match 'real' to the upright image and 'virtual' to the inverted one.
misconceptions.correction: Real and virtual are about where the light goes, not about appearance. A real image can be caught on a screen and is inverted; the upright images produced by lenses are the virtual ones.

misconceptions.question: Should I draw the real curved shape of the lens in a ray diagram?
misconceptions.correct: No. In ray diagrams a convex lens is represented by a vertical straight line with outward arrowheads, and a concave lens by one with inward arrowheads.
misconceptions.misconception: A ray diagram should show the lens as it really looks, curved on both faces, with the rays bending at each curved surface.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are taught, correctly, that a lens is thicker or thinner in the middle and that light is refracted at each surface, so drawing the true shape feels more honest than a straight line. Photographs and cut-away diagrams of lenses reinforce the picture.
misconceptions.correction: The straight-line symbol with arrowheads is the convention the specification sets out, and it is what examiners expect. All the refraction is treated as happening in a single step at that line, which is why the standard ray rules give the right image position.

mcqs.stem: A beam of rays travelling parallel to the principal axis passes through a convex lens. What happens to the rays?

options.text: They are reflected from the lens surface to a point in front
options.rationale: A student who thinks a lens works like a mirror expects the light to bounce off the front surface rather than pass through it.

options.text: They are refracted so that they meet at the principal focus
options.rationale: This is the definition given in the specification: in a convex lens, parallel rays of light are brought to a focus at the principal focus.

options.text: They are refracted so that they meet at the focal length
options.rationale: This confuses the point with the distance: the focal length is the distance from the lens to the principal focus, not a place where rays meet.

options.text: They carry straight on, since they strike the lens head-on
options.rationale: A student who thinks light bends only at one surface, or only when it arrives at an angle, expects rays along the axis direction to pass through unchanged.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the focal length of a convex lens?

options.text: The distance from the lens to the image it produces
options.rationale: Students measure a lens-to-screen distance in practical work and take that to be the focal length; it only matches for a very distant object.

options.text: The distance the object must be to give a sharp image
options.rationale: Focusing a camera or magnifier is an experience of moving the object, so 'focal' becomes attached to the object distance.

options.text: The distance from the lens to the principal focus
options.rationale: This is exactly how the specification defines the focal length.

options.text: The length of the lens across its widest part
options.rationale: A reasonable reading of the everyday word 'length' as a measurement of the lens itself rather than of a distance in the ray diagram.

mcqs.stem: A lens forms an image. Where is the light changed in direction?

options.text: It is reflected from both surfaces of the lens
options.rationale: A student who pictures a lens as a kind of mirror expects the image to be made by light bouncing off it.

options.text: It is refracted only at the surface where it leaves
options.rationale: Diagrams usually hide the path inside the glass, so students see a single bend at the far side.

options.text: It is diffracted as it spreads out inside the glass
options.rationale: Diffraction is another word met in the waves topic, and 'spreading out' sounds like what a lens does to a beam.

options.text: It is refracted as it enters and as it leaves the lens
options.rationale: A lens forms an image by refracting light, and refraction occurs at each boundary the light crosses.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the image produced by a concave lens is correct?

options.text: It is real when the object is beyond the principal focus
options.rationale: This transfers the convex lens rule, where object position does decide whether the image is real or virtual.

options.text: It is real and inverted, like a convex lens image
options.rationale: The inverted real image of a convex lens is the most memorable result, so it is applied to every lens.

options.text: It is virtual only when the object is close to the lens
options.rationale: This sounds cautious and rule-like, and mirrors the 'inside the focus' condition students meet for the convex lens.

options.text: It is always virtual, whatever the object distance
options.rationale: The specification states without exception that the image produced by a concave lens is always virtual.

mcqs.stem: An object is placed between a convex lens and its principal focus. What kind of image is formed?

options.text: A real image, inverted and larger than the object
options.rationale: A student who believes a convex lens always gives a real, inverted image keeps those two properties and only adjusts the size.

options.text: A virtual image, upright and larger than the object
options.rationale: The refracted rays leave still diverging, so they never meet; traced back they give an upright, magnified virtual image. This is the magnifying glass.

options.text: A virtual image, upright and smaller than the object
options.rationale: A student who thinks all virtual images are diminished applies the concave lens result to the convex lens.

options.text: A real image, inverted and smaller than the object
options.rationale: This is the correct answer for an object beyond twice the focal length, recalled without checking where the object actually is.

mcqs.stem: Which observation shows that an image formed by a lens is real rather than virtual?

options.text: It can be seen by an eye that looks through the lens
options.rationale: A student who thinks a virtual image cannot be seen treats visibility as the test for a real image.

options.text: It is the same way up as the object that produced it
options.rationale: 'Real' is read as 'true to life', so the upright image is taken to be the real one; in fact a real lens image is inverted.

options.text: It is smaller than the object that produced it
options.rationale: Size is confused with the real/virtual distinction; a real image may be larger, smaller or the same size.

options.text: It can be formed on a screen placed where the rays meet
options.rationale: A real image is formed where light rays actually meet, so light really arrives at the screen and a picture appears on it.

mcqs.stem: In a ray diagram for a convex lens, how is the ray from the top of the object to the centre of the lens drawn?

options.text: It is refracted towards the principal focus
options.rationale: A student who believes every ray must be bent applies the parallel-ray rule to the central ray as well.

options.text: It is refracted so that it leaves parallel to the axis
options.rationale: This is the rule for a ray that passes through the principal focus on the object side, applied to the wrong ray.

options.text: It carries straight on without changing direction
options.rationale: At the centre the two surfaces are parallel, so the ray emerges in its original direction; this straight ray fixes the image position.

options.text: It is reflected back along the path it came
options.rationale: Only a student picturing the lens as a mirror would send the ray back the way it came.

mcqs.stem: In a ray diagram for a concave lens, a ray arrives parallel to the principal axis. How is it drawn after the lens?

options.text: It converges to the principal focus beyond the lens
options.rationale: This is the convex lens rule, learned first and reused because the two diagrams look alike.

options.text: It carries straight on, since the lens cannot focus it
options.rationale: A student who links refraction only with focusing concludes that a diverging lens leaves the ray unchanged.

options.text: It diverges, as if it had come from the principal focus
options.rationale: A concave lens spreads light apart; traced backwards the refracted ray passes through the principal focus on the object side, which is why the image is virtual.

options.text: It travels back towards the object along the same path
options.rationale: Sending the ray back the way it came treats the lens as a reflecting surface.

mcqs.stem: A student draws ray diagrams for a convex lens and a concave lens using the same object. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: Both refract the light, but only the convex lens converges it
options.rationale: The similarity is the mechanism — both form images by refraction — and the difference is that the convex lens brings parallel rays to a focus while the concave lens spreads them.

options.text: Both refract the light, and both can produce a real image
options.rationale: A student who thinks a concave lens can converge light at some object distance expects a real image from it.

options.text: Only the convex lens refracts light, the concave one reflects
options.rationale: Confusing the diverging action of a concave lens with light bouncing back off it.

options.text: Both produce virtual images, but the convex one is inverted
options.rationale: This keeps 'lenses invert images' and attaches it to the wrong lens, while wrongly ruling out real images altogether.

mcqs.stem: An object 5 mm tall produces an image 15 mm tall. What is the magnification?

options.rationale: Dividing object height by image height, 5/15, inverts the equation.
magnification = image height / object height = 15 mm / 5 mm = 3.

options.text: 3 mm
options.rationale: The arithmetic is right but a unit has been attached; the mm cancel, so magnification has no unit.
Subtracting the heights, 15 − 5, instead of dividing them.

mcqs.stem: An object 8.0 cm tall produces an image 2.4 cm tall. What is the magnification?

options.rationale: Dividing the larger height by the smaller to force an answer above 1, in the belief that magnification must enlarge.

options.text: 0.3 cm
options.rationale: Correct arithmetic spoiled by adding a unit to a ratio.
Multiplying the two heights instead of dividing them.
magnification = image height / object height = 2.4 cm / 8.0 cm = 0.3, a number below 1 because the image is smaller.

mcqs.stem: An object 40 mm tall produces an image 8.0 cm tall. What is the magnification?

options.rationale: Dividing 8.0 by 40 without converting, so a cm value is divided by a mm value.
Converting correctly but then dividing object height by image height, 40/80.
Convert first: 8.0 cm = 80 mm, so magnification = 80 mm / 40 mm = 2.
Dividing 40 by 8.0: the equation is inverted and the units are left unconverted.

mcqs.stem: How should the magnification produced by a lens be written?

options.text: As a number on its own, since it is a ratio
options.rationale: Magnification is a ratio and so has no units: a height divided by a height leaves a pure number.

options.text: In centimetres, since heights are given in cm
options.rationale: Students are trained to put a unit on every answer and carry the height unit through.

options.text: In millimetres, since the ruler reads in mm
options.rationale: The same habit, taking the unit from the measuring instrument used.

options.text: As a number greater than 1, since images grow
options.rationale: 'Magnify' means enlarge in everyday speech, so values below 1 are assumed to be errors.

mcqs.stem: In ray diagrams, which symbol is used to represent a convex lens?

options.text: A vertical line with an arrowhead at each end pointing inwards
options.rationale: This is the concave lens symbol, chosen by a student who reads inward arrows as light being brought to a focus.

options.text: A vertical line with an arrowhead at each end pointing outwards
options.rationale: This is the symbol the specification gives for a convex lens; the outward arrowheads match a lens that is thicker in the middle.

options.text: A vertical line with a single arrowhead at its upper end only
options.rationale: An upright single-headed arrow is how the object is drawn in a ray diagram, so it is easily confused with the lens.

options.text: A curved line that bulges outwards on both of its two faces
options.rationale: A student who believes the true cross-section should be drawn picks the curved shape; ray diagrams use the straight-line symbol instead.

mcqs.stem: A ray diagram shows a vertical line with an arrowhead at each end pointing inwards. Which lens is this, and what does it do to parallel rays?

options.text: A concave lens, which spreads parallel rays apart
options.rationale: Inward arrowheads represent the concave lens, which is thinner in the middle and diverges parallel rays.

options.text: A convex lens, which brings parallel rays to a focus
options.rationale: The symbol has been read as convex; the description of what a convex lens does is itself correct.

options.text: A convex lens, which spreads parallel rays apart
options.rationale: The symbol is misread and the action is wrong as well, but each half looks familiar in isolation.

options.text: A concave lens, which brings parallel rays to a focus
options.rationale: The symbol is read correctly but the convex ray rule is applied to it, exactly the error made in concave ray diagrams.
